title: How Antiques Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how antiques work: the origins of popular antiques interest (Herculaneum and Pompeii excavations, the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia), the roughly 1830 cutoff tied to the Industrial Revolution and mass manufacturing, and reproduction versus period furniture. They cover how to date and authenticate pieces by construction (dovetail and mortise-and-tenon joints, hand-made versus machine-cut nails, saw marks, staples, plywood), wood types (walnut, mahogany, cherry, oak, pine, Florida heart pine), shrinkage, and maker's marks and provenance. They discuss the Brewster chair hoax and the film F for Fake, how value is set by what buyers will pay, where to buy (museums, antique stores, flea markets, auctions, estate and yard sales, eBay), and how to care for antiques. Paul Brown of Gallery 63 and Auction Kings is interviewed. The episode closes with a listener mail about polyamory and a sign-off asking for listener stories about finds in attics.

segments.title: Opening banter and antiques trivia
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on antiques and mention the link to the Volcanoes episode through Herculaneum and Pompeii, and the 1876 Philadelphia centennial that sparked American interest in antiques.

segments.title: Origins of antiques popularity
segments.summary: Discussion of how the Vesuvius-buried cities were excavated under Charles III of Spain and sparked neoclassical interest, and how the 1876 Philadelphia exhibition kindled American interest in early American furniture.

segments.title: Antique cutoff date and reproductions
segments.summary: Purists treat pre-1830 items as antiques, a date tied to the Industrial Revolution and mass manufacturing. Mass production led to reproduction furniture, distinguished from period pieces made in a given style.

segments.title: Judging condition and construction
segments.summary: Paul Brown's tips for spotting a real antique: overall condition, high-quality fakes being rare, and construction clues such as dovetail and mortise-and-tenon joints versus nails, and evenly cut nails indicating later manufacture.

segments.title: Wood types, shrinkage and saw marks
segments.summary: Walnut, mahogany, cherry, oak and pine are discussed as clues to age and period, including Florida heart pine salvaged from the river. Shrinkage, pegs, plywood and staples are noted as signs of later manufacture, and saw marks can roughly date a piece.

segments.title: Value and buying at auction
segments.summary: Paul Brown says value is what someone will pay on a given day, driven by how many buyers want an item. Buy only what you like, and treat auctions as an experience; preview before bidding.

segments.title: Brewster chair hoax and art forgery
segments.summary: The Brewster chair, faked by Lamont and displayed at the Ford Museum, is described as a famous antique hoax. The film F for Fake and the forger Elmyr and biographer Clifford Irving are discussed, making the point that experts can be fooled.

segments.title: Where to buy antiques and provenance
segments.summary: Places to buy include small-town antique stores, flea markets, estate and yard sales, eBay, and antique shows. Maker's marks and documentation such as photos and letters boost value, illustrated by a Kit Carson blanket story from Antiques Roadshow.

segments.title: Caring for antiques
segments.summary: Advice on maintaining antiques: winding clocks, displaying rugs, storing books upright away from acidic paper and sun, and storing photographs in individual envelopes.

segments.title: Listener mail on polyamory
segments.summary: A listener from Saskatoon describes her polyamorous relationship with two partners, covering their arrangements, STI testing, and family and friends' acceptance.

segments.title: Sign-off and listener request
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to send stories of valuable finds from attics and mention the website and podcast app.
